name: S-23
lead: S-23, also called Mastorin, is an investigational selective androgen receptor modulator (SARM) developed by GTx, Inc. as a candidate male hormonal contraceptive [1]. It is a nonsteroidal compound that binds the androgen receptor more tightly than the older SARM andarine, with a reported Ki of 1.7 nM [1]. People interested in physique change take an interest in SARMs because androgen receptor activation in muscle and bone is associated with more lean mass and less fat, the route to a more muscular, leaner look [2][3].

The main preclinical study, published in Endocrinology in 2009, tested S-23 in male rats. It found that S-23 bound the androgen receptor strongly and acted as a full agonist, that combined with estradiol benzoate it suppressed LH and FSH and eliminated sperm in most animals, and that fertility recovered fully after treatment ended. The same study reported increased bone density and lean mass and reduced fat mass in the animals [3].

S-23 has not been approved for any use and no published human trial describes it. It is listed as an Investigational New Drug in the United States, and it appeared by 2020 as a designer drug sold online as a research chemical [1]. SARMs as a class are prohibited by the World Anti-Doping Agency, and S-23 was involved in five adverse analytical findings in doping control in 2022 [4][2].

angle.text: Physique-focused users are interested in S-23 for the anabolic effects reported in animal studies, where it increased lean mass and reduced fat mass in male rats [3]. Whether this carries over to people has not been tested in published human trials.

paras: S-23 has no approved medical use. It was developed to explore an oral male contraceptive that would suppress sperm production while maintaining androgenic effects [1][3]. Outside that research, it is sold online as a research chemical and discussed alongside other SARMs in muscle-building communities [1][5].

S-23 is a nonsteroidal androgen receptor ligand (formula C18H13ClF4N2O3) with higher affinity than andarine [1]. Its preclinical characterisation was published by Jones and colleagues in 2009; in rats it acted as a full agonist and the findings included lower fat mass, higher lean mass and higher bone density [3]. The chemistry of this family of metabolically stable SARMs was described by Marhefka and colleagues in 2004 in the Journal of Medicinal Chemistry [1].

A 2025 doping-control study dosed volunteers with microdoses of S-23 and identified 18 urinary metabolites. A single 1 microgram dose remained detectable for about 253 hours on average and a 50 microgram dose for about 544 hours [4].

No human safety data exist for S-23 specifically. For SARMs as a class, a 2024 analysis in the European Journal of Clinical Pharmacology identified 20 published adverse-event reports since 2020, mostly drug-induced liver injury, and noted that none is approved by the FDA or EMA [6]. Class-level effects described in the literature include raised liver enzymes, lower HDL cholesterol and suppression of testosterone [2].

A 2024 analysis of 13 SARM products bought online from Italy found the labelled SARM in about 70% of samples, a different SARM in 23%, and undeclared pharmaceutical substances such as tamoxifen, clomifene and testosterone in about 30%. Quantified content ranged from 30% to 90% of the label claim [5].

SARMs were prohibited by the World Anti-Doping Agency in 2008 [2]. Small laboratories sell them online as research chemicals, and products have been reported to be mislabeled [2][5]. The Italian product study noted that many websites described products as for research only while giving dosing and training guidance [5].

No studies found in humans. The published research on S-23 is a rat study of its use for male contraception, which also reported effects on lean mass, fat mass and bone density [3], and a doping-control study of urinary metabolites [4]. Related research on other SARMs includes enobosarm, which a Phase III trial found increased lean body mass without a significant improvement in physical function [2].

card.summary: An investigational nonsteroidal SARM developed as a male contraceptive candidate; no human trials are published and it appears as a gray-market research chemical.
card.note: Investigational only; no published human studies; sold as a designer drug.

quick.overview:
S-23 is an experimental selective androgen receptor modulator (SARM) developed by GTx, Inc. as a possible male hormonal contraceptive. It binds the androgen receptor more tightly than the older SARM andarine.

Its appearance relevance comes from the broader SARM category, which is used in muscle-building circles. No human trials of S-23 are described in the sources consulted.
quick.mechanism: It is a nonsteroidal compound that binds the androgen receptor (reported Ki of about 1.7 nM). In animal work it was reported to suppress spermatogenesis in a dose-dependent way, with recovery after treatment stopped.
quick.risks: No human safety data are described. SARMs as a class are banned by WADA, and compounds sold online as research chemicals have been reported to be mislabeled. Class-level reports include liver enzyme elevation and suppression of the body's own testosterone production.
